title: Episode 80: The Lost Colony of Roanoke: The Vanished Settlers of 1587
description:
The Lost Colony of Roanoke: The Vanished Settlers of 1587. How America's first English settlement on the barrier islands of North Carolina disappeared into the wilderness during the Anglo-Spanish War, leaving the riddle of CROATOAN. Join Rebecca and George for an immersive historical deep dive into the mystery of Roanoke.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome back to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. In the hot summer of 1587, on a lonely, wind-scoured barrier island off the coast of North Carolina, one hundred and fifteen English pioneers landed to establish the first permanent English settlement in the New World. Among them was Eleanor Dare, who gave birth to Virginia Dare, the first English child born in the Americas. When their governor, John White, returned three years later after being trapped in England by the Spanish Armada, the settlement was deserted. The palisade was dismantled, the houses were gone, and carved into a cedar post at the entrance were five haunting letters: C-R-O. On a nearby tree trunk was carved the full word: CROATOAN. George brings us the timeless mystery of the Lost Colony of Roanoke.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: SIR WALTER RALEIGH AND THE ISLAND OF ROANOKE
In the late sixteenth century, Queen Elizabeth the First of England sought to challenge the sprawling global empire of Catholic Spain by establishing Protestant colonies in the New World. English privateer and royal favorite Sir Walter Raleigh was granted a royal charter to discover and plant colonies on lands not owned by any Christian prince. In fifteen eighty-four, Raleigh dispatched an exploratory expedition commanded by Philip Amadas and Arthur Barlowe, who scouted the Outer Banks of North Carolina and returned with glowing reports of fragrant cedar forests, sweet grapes, and welcoming Indigenous tribes. The following year, Raleigh sent a military expedition commanded by Sir Richard Grenville and Governor Ralph Lane to fortify Roanoke Island. But Lane was an arrogant, aggressive soldier who alienated the neighboring Secotan people, burned a native village over a missing silver cup, and executed the local chieftain Wingina. When privateer Sir Francis Drake stopped at Roanoke in fifteen eighty-six after raiding Spanish Caribbean ports, the starving, demoralized soldiers begged him for transport back to England, abandoning the settlement and leaving the island empty once more. Amadas and Barlowe brought two Native ambassadors—Wanchese of the Roanoke and Manteo of the Croatan—back to London, where their exotic presence at court dazzled the Elizabethan nobility and helped secure royal investment for colonization. The English court viewed the Carolina coast as a strategic sanctuary from which privateers could ambush Spanish treasure fleets sailing north along the Gulf Stream, prioritizing imperial rivalry over peaceful agricultural settlement.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE CITY OF RALEGH IN VIRGINIA
Raleigh learned from the failure of Lane's military garrison that an enduring colony required permanent families rather than mercenaries. In fifteen eighty-seven, Raleigh recruited one hundred and fifteen civilian settlers: eighty-nine men, seventeen women, and nine young children, composed of tradesmen, farmers, tailors, and merchants who paid their own passage in exchange for five hundred acres of free land. Raleigh appointed artist and explorer John White as governor, accompanied by twelve assistants. White was instructed to bypass Roanoke entirely and sail further north into the sheltered, deep-water Chesapeake Bay. But when their three ships arrived at Roanoke Island in July fifteen eighty-seven to check on a small caretaker garrison of fifteen soldiers, Portuguese pilot Simon Fernandes refused to sail any further, ordering the colonists ashore in the swampy heat of midsummer. Reluctantly, the settlers moved into the dilapidated wooden cottages built by Lane's garrison, repairing thatch roofs, clearing overgrown gardens, and preparing to build their lives on the sandy island. Simon Fernandes was a former Portuguese privateer with a shadowy past who feuded bitterly with Governor White throughout the Atlantic crossing, caring far more about hunting Spanish treasure galleons in the West Indies than the survival of English homesteaders. Settlers repaired the cedar roof shingles and planted English peas and barley, hoping that honest labor would overcome the hostile frontier wilderness and establish a permanent haven for Protestant England.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: VIRGINIA DARE AND THE LOOMING CRISIS
On August eighteenth, fifteen eighty-seven, an event of profound historical significance occurred in the colony: Eleanor Dare, the governor's daughter, gave birth to a healthy baby girl. Baptized on the following Sunday as Virginia Dare, she was celebrated as the first English child born on the soil of the Americas. But the colonists' joy was swiftly eclipsed by mounting peril. The fifteen caretaker soldiers had been murdered by hostile mainland tribes seeking vengeance for Ralph Lane's earlier cruelties. When colonist George Howe was ambushed and killed by Secotan warriors while catching crabs in the shallow sounds, the settlers realized they were surrounded by bitter enemies and cut off from supplies. The crops they planted were meager, the sandy soil was poor, and winter was approaching. The colonists pleaded with Governor John White to return immediately to England aboard Fernandes's ships to secure emergency food, cattle, tools, and reinforcements. White hesitated, reluctant to abandon his daughter and newborn granddaughter, but the colonists insisted, signing an official covenant promising to safeguard the settlement. The birth of Virginia Dare was celebrated with the firing of celebratory arquebus volleys, but the joy was shadowed by the constant terror of night raids from the mainland Secotan warriors who had sworn to destroy the English settlement. Eleanor Dare clutched her newborn infant daughter in the dark blockhouse, praying that the relief fleet would return from Plymouth before their winter provisions of salted beef and oatmeal were exhausted.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE SPANISH ARMADA AND THREE YEARS OF TORMENT
When John White arrived back in England in November fifteen eighty-seven, he was met by a national emergency that doomed his rescue mission. King Philip the Second of Spain had assembled the invincible Spanish Armada—one hundred and thirty massive galleons carrying thirty thousand soldiers—to invade England, dethrone Queen Elizabeth, and re-establish Catholicism. Queen Elizabeth declared a naval embargo, requisitioning every English ship, captain, and barrel of powder for national defense. For three agonizing years, John White was trapped in London and Plymouth, watching helplessly as his relief ships were diverted to combat. White paced the docks in despair, knowing his family on Roanoke was running out of food. It was not until the summer of fifteen ninety, two years after the Royal Navy shattered the Armada in the English Channel, that White finally secured passage aboard two privateering vessels, the Hopewell and the Moonlight, bound for the Caribbean and the Carolina Outer Banks. White petitioned Sir Walter Raleigh, Lord Burghley, and the Queen Privy Council repeatedly, but the threat of a Catholic Spanish invasion paralyzed the nation, leaving all Atlantic merchant shipping locked in English coastal harbors under royal decree. White attended meetings with Queen Elizabeth ministers, describing the desperate plight of the Roanoke families, but every timber and pound of canvas in England was committed to repelling the Spanish invasion.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE SILENT ISLAND AND THE CRYPTIC POST
On the evening of August fifteenth, fifteen ninety, White's ships dropped anchor off the treacherous shoals of Roanoke Island. As darkness fell, sailors spotted columns of smoke rising from the dunes, cheering at what they believed was a welcoming campfire. But when White's longboat reached the beach the following morning, they found only burning brush with no human tracks. Rowing inland toward the settlement, sailors sounded trumpets and sang English folk songs into the heavy forest, but met only eerie silence. Climbing the sandy bluff to the palisade, White was shocked: the houses had been taken down, and the entire perimeter was enclosed by a stout wooden palisade of heavy tree trunks. The colony was deserted. Carved into a tall cedar post by the entrance gate were three capital letters: C-R-O. On an unbarked pine trunk near the trench, carved in neat Roman letters five feet above the ground, was the full word: CROATOAN. Before leaving in fifteen eighty-seven, White and the colonists had agreed that if they relocated, they would carve their new location on a tree, and if they were in distress, they would carve a Maltese cross above the name. There was no cross. White and his sailors examined the palisade posts carefully, noting that the letters were carved neatly and deliberately with an iron chisel, indicating that the departure had been orderly and planned rather than the result of a sudden violent massacre. The absence of any cross carved above the word Croatoan brought immense relief to White, confirming that his family had not been attacked or slaughtered, but had relocated in search of food.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE BURIED CHESTS AND THE RISING GALE
White searched the abandoned clearing frantically, discovering that the colonists had buried heavy chests and armor in the sand before departing. But Indigenous scavengers had unearthed the caches, scattering White's personal books, maps, and family heirlooms across the dirt, shredded by rain and trampling feet. Croatoan was the name of a barrier island fifty miles to the south—modern-day Hatteras Island—home to the friendly Croatan tribe led by Chief Manteo, who had traveled to London with White years earlier and was baptized into the Church of England. Convinced his daughter and granddaughter were living safely among Manteo's people, White hurried back to the ships, pleading with the captains to hoist sail for Croatoan immediately. But a violent Atlantic gale swept across the Outer Banks, snapping the Hopewell's anchor cables, grounding longboats, and destroying their drinking water casks. Low on provisions and facing hurricane-force winds, the privateering captain refused to risk his vessel, steering the ship eastward across the stormy Atlantic back to England. John White died in Ireland three years later, brokenhearted and penniless, having never laid eyes on his daughter or granddaughter again. The privateering captains had little sympathy for White family, driven solely by the pursuit of Spanish prize ships in the Caribbean and eager to flee the treacherous Outer Banks sandbars before a full Atlantic hurricane destroyed their vessels. The violent autumn storm shattered the longboats and drowned seven sailors in the roaring surf, forcing the ships to abandon the search and steer eastward into the vast, stormy Atlantic.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE LEGACY AND THE LUMBEE PEOPLE
For over four centuries, the fate of the Lost Colony of Roanoke has captivated historians, archaeologists, and storytellers as America's greatest unsolved mystery. When Jamestown was founded in sixteen oh-seven, Captain John Smith heard rumors from Powhatan chieftains of white men living in stone houses and dressing in European clothing deep in the Carolina interior. Subsequent explorers in the eighteenth century encountered Native tribes along the Lumbee River in North Carolina—the ancestors of today's Lumbee Tribe—who possessed gray eyes, European features, spoke archaic Elizabethan English, and shared family surnames found on John White's original roster, including Dare, Sampson, and Brooks. Modern archaeological excavations by the First Colony Foundation have unearthed Elizabethan pottery shards, gunflints, and copper trade rings at 'Site X' in Bertie County on the Albemarle Sound, suggesting that the colonists integrated into native communities and survived through cultural synthesis. Today, on the shores of Roanoke Island, the historic drama The Lost Colony plays under the summer stars, keeping alive the memory of one hundred and fifteen brave souls whose disappearance marks the mysterious, haunting dawn of English America. Over the centuries, countless theories have been proposed to explain the colony fate, but the most enduring and supported hypothesis remains that the English settlers were absorbed into neighboring Native communities, where their bloodlines continue to this day. The story of the Lost Colony of Roanoke remains an enduring testament to the courage of the ordinary families who ventured into the unknown, leaving behind a haunting enigma that still echoes across the Carolina dunes.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
The riddle of CROATOAN whispers across the dunes of North Carolina, a timeless reminder of the courage and fragility of America's first pioneers. I'm Rebecca. Join us next week as we board pirate sloops off Ocracoke Inlet for the legendary final stand of Blackbeard.
